title: Bonds & Debt
blurb: Bonds and debt funds: how they pay, what moves their price, and how to explain risk without jargon.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays, niche topics); investors as awareness material
About 87 minutes of lessons, plus role-play and the final quiz
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway

sources: SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds (current edition)
SEBI circular on Potential Risk Class (PRC) matrix for debt schemes (2021)

lessons.title: A bond is a loan: issuer, face value, coupon, maturity, price, yield
SEBI debt categories by time: the duration ladder
SEBI debt categories by borrower, plus target maturity funds
The three debt risks, plus a quiet fourth
Matching the need to the option
Checklist before recommending, and debt-fund tax
Reading a debt fund: monthly factsheet checks
Rate cycles, rebalancing and red flags
Niche topics (1): side-pocketing, AT1, calls and ratings

a: A loan you give to a government or company. You earn interest (coupon) and get the face value back at maturity.
Fixed interest paid on face value. ₹1,000 bond at 7% pays ₹70 a year.
When interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall; when rates fall, prices rise.
Yield to Maturity: yearly return if bought today and held to maturity. Indicative, before fund expenses; not a promise.
Short-term government borrowing (91, 182 or 364 days). Issued at a discount, repaid at face value; no coupon.
Invests in securities maturing up to 91 days. For emergency money and short-term parking.
Invests in securities maturing in 1 day. Lowest interest-rate risk.
At least 80% in government securities. No credit risk, but can swing with interest rates.
At least 80% in corporate bonds rated AA+ and above.
At least 65% in bonds rated AA and below. Higher yield for higher default risk.
At least 80% in debt of banks, PSUs and public financial institutions.
Portfolio Macaulay duration of 1–3 years. Suits goals 1–3 years away.
Portfolio Macaulay duration above 7 years. Large swings when rates move.
SEBI's 3×3 grid showing a debt scheme's maximum interest-rate risk (Class I–III) and credit risk (A–C). A-I is the most conservative.
Gains on debt funds bought on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rate with no indexation. Confirm with a CA.
A SEBI-registered platform for buying listed bonds directly; many bonds now available from ₹10,000 face value.
Bond prices fall when rates rise.
Example: Gilt fund NAV dips after a rate hike
Remember: Match duration to the goal date.
The borrower delays, fails to pay or is downgraded.
Example: IL&FS default in 2018 hit several debt funds
Remember: Stick to high ratings; don't chase yield.
Bonds can't be sold quickly at a fair price.
Example: Franklin Templeton wound up six debt schemes in 2020
Remember: Prefer liquid categories and diversified funds.
Maturing money may have to be reinvested at lower rates.
Example: FD renewing at a lower rate
Remember: A bond ladder smooths it.
Approximate price change for a 1% move in rates.
Example: Duration 8: rates up 1% → price ≈ −8%
Remember: Shorter duration for nearer goals.
Weighted-average time to receive a bond's cash flows, in years.
Example: Used for SEBI's duration categories
Remember: Use it to match the goal date.
An agency's opinion of a borrower's ability to repay. AAA is highest.
Example: Rating outlook "negative" = early warning
Remember: Ratings can change fast.
A passive fund holding bonds that mature around one date.
Example: A fund tracking a 2030 bond index
Remember: Held to maturity, return ≈ starting YTM after costs; not guaranteed.
A defaulted bond is moved to a separate portfolio; investors get units in both.
Example: Recovery, if any, is paid out later
Remember: The side-pocket can't be redeemed early.
Bank bond with no maturity; can skip interest or be written off.
Example: Yes Bank AT1 bonds written off in 2020
Remember: Never a substitute for an FD.
The issuer can repay early; Yield to Call shows the return if it does.
Example: Issuer calls the bond after rates fall
Remember: Investor must reinvest at lower rates.
Extra yield a corporate bond pays over a G-sec of the same maturity.
Example: AAA corporate at 7.6% vs G-sec at 7.0% → 0.6% spread (illustrative)
Remember: Wider spread = more perceived risk.
Yields plotted against maturity. Normal: longer pays more.
Example: Flat curve = little extra pay for lending longer
Remember: Shows whether longer maturities are rewarded.
Clean excludes accrued interest; dirty includes it and is what the buyer pays.
Example: Quoted ₹1,000, paid ₹1,017
Remember: Explains price differences on bond platforms.
Money spread across bonds or FDs maturing in different years.
Example: ₹5 L each maturing in years 1–5
Remember: Regular maturities for income; less reinvestment risk.
Capital gains bonds from specified issuers with a 5-year lock-in.
Example: Used after selling property
Remember: Confirm eligibility and limits with a CA.

questions.q: When interest rates rise, existing bond prices:
questions.why: Fall. The price–yield seesaw.

questions.q: A ₹1,000 bond with a 7% coupon pays each year:
questions.why: ₹70. Coupon is interest on face value.

questions.q: Liquid funds invest in securities maturing up to:
questions.why: 91 days. Overnight funds: 1 day.

questions.q: Gilt funds must hold at least 80% in:
questions.why: Government securities. No credit risk, but rate risk remains.

questions.q: Credit risk funds hold at least 65% in bonds rated:
questions.why: AA and below. Higher yield for higher default risk.

questions.q: A fund with modified duration 6 will, if rates fall 1%, roughly:
questions.why: Rise 6%. Price moves opposite to rates by about the duration.

questions.q: The most conservative cell in the PRC matrix is:
questions.why: A-I. Low credit risk, duration up to 1 year.

questions.q: Which risk caused sudden NAV drops when IL&FS defaulted in 2018?
questions.why: Credit risk. The borrower defaulted.

questions.q: A T-bill pays:
o: No coupon; issued at a discount
questions.why: No coupon; issued at a discount. Repaid at face value.

questions.q: Side-pocketing is used when:
o: A held bond suffers a severe credit event
questions.why: A held bond suffers a severe credit event. Separates the troubled bond from the main portfolio.

questions.q: For money a client may need any day, the usual choice is:
questions.why: Liquid or overnight fund. Lowest rate and credit risk, high liquidity.

questions.q: For a goal 1–3 years away, a suitable category is:
questions.why: Short duration. Duration matched to the goal.

questions.q: What happened to Yes Bank's AT1 bonds in 2020?
questions.why: Written off. AT1 holders lost their investment.

questions.q: For debt funds bought from 1 April 2023, gains are generally taxed:
o: Only on maturity of each bond
questions.why: At slab rate, without indexation. Confirm specifics with the client's CA.

questions.q: The PRC matrix shows a debt scheme's:
questions.why: Maximum interest-rate and credit risk. The riskometer shows today's portfolio risk.

questions.q: G-secs have no default risk. What risk remains if sold before maturity?
o: Interest-rate risk: prices fall when rates rise
questions.why: Rate risk remains.

questions.q: A debt fund's YTM is much higher than its peers'. What should you check first?
o: Whether it means lower credit quality or longer duration
questions.why: Higher yield often means more credit or duration risk.

questions.q: What can happen to AT1 bonds if the bank is in trouble?
questions.why: As happened with Yes Bank in 2020.

questions.q: For a goal 2 years away, which duration fits best?
o: Short duration, matched to the goal date
Any duration, if the yield is high
Duration does not matter for debt
questions.why: Choose short duration to match the goal date.

questions.q: Held to maturity, a target maturity fund's return is usually:
o: Close to its YTM at purchase, after costs
Equal to the equity market return
questions.why: Not guaranteed; early exit changes the outcome.

questions.q: A client says, “My debt fund fell 2% this month. I thought debt was safe.” How do you respond?
o: Promise a recovery by next month
Check whether it is a rate move or a credit event; explain duration and the seesaw; review duration vs goal; no promise of recovery
questions.why: Checks whether it is a rate move or a credit event; explains duration and the seesaw; reviews duration vs goal; no promise of recovery.

questions.q: A client wants to move all their FD money into a credit risk fund showing a 9% yield. What do you explain?
o: The yield–risk trade-off; default and liquidity risk; sizing as a small slice at most; not for essential money
That credit risk funds never default
questions.why: Yield–risk trade-off; default and liquidity risk; sizing as a small slice at most; not for essential money.

questions.q: A retiree wants monthly income from ₹60 lakh. What do you outline?
o: SWP from a conservative debt fund, a bond ladder, and eligible government schemes; check current rates rather than quoting from memory; tax via CA
A credit risk fund for the full amount
An equity fund for regular income
questions.why: SWP from a conservative debt fund, bond ladder, eligible government schemes; checks current rates rather than quoting from memory; tax via CA.

questions.q: A parent needs college fees in 2 years. Which debt category fits and why?
o: Short duration / banking & PSU / matched target maturity; long duration and credit risk don’t fit a 2-year goal
Any category, since 2 years is long enough
questions.why: Short duration / banking & PSU / matched target maturity; explains why long duration and credit risk don't fit.

questions.q: A client sees a “bank bond at 10%” online. What do you check and say?
o: Nothing — a bank bond is safe
Whether it is an AT1/perpetual bond, its rating and the platform’s registration; explain write-off risk; it is not an FD substitute
questions.why: Checks if it is an AT1/perpetual bond, rating and platform registration; explains write-off risk; not an FD substitute.
